explanations.explanation: That's the list, baker. Genesis 13:2 says Abram had become extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold. Cows, sheep, shiny coins and bars of gold. I once had a price sticker and a mustache, so I'm taking notes.

Spices and fine linen sound fancy, but they're not on the list. The text says Abram had become extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold (Genesis 13:2). So no perfume shop, just herds and shiny metal. Picture a very busy pasture with a very heavy wallet.

Land and vineyards would be a nice portfolio, but that's not what the verse says. Genesis 13:2 says Abram had become extremely wealthy in livestock and silver and gold. Notice he's still moving his tent around, so he's got herds, not a deed. Animals you can walk, and land you can't.

True! Genesis 13:4 says Abram built the altar there, and that's where he called on the name of the LORD. He came all this way and went right back to the spot where he'd worshiped before. I love that. When I get back to my bakery, the first thing I do is thank Him too.

Not quite, friend. The text says Abram returned to the site where he had built the altar, and there he called on the name of the LORD (Genesis 13:4). So the altar is not just a landmark. It's where he prays. Think of it like the one spot in your kitchen where you always find your keys, except way holier.

Look at what the text says, baker. It says the land was unable to support both of them while they stayed together (Genesis 13:6). So there wasn't plenty of room, it was crowded. Two huge households and one stretch of land makes for a very tight squeeze.

False is right! Genesis 13:6 says the land was unable to support both of them while they stayed together, because they had so many possessions. They couldn't coexist. It's like two people trying to fit one oven rack's worth of cookies on one tray. Something's gotta give.

Yes, Lot, Abram's nephew. Genesis 13:7 says there was discord between the herdsmen of Abram and the herdsmen of Lot. The two men's workers were bumping into each other all day. That's a lot of animals and a lot of attitude.

Pharaoh, Egypt's king, is back in the last chapter, not in this fight. Abram has already left Egypt (Genesis 13:1). The discord is between the herdsmen of Abram and the herdsmen of Lot (Genesis 13:7). This one's a family matter.

Laban doesn't show up in this passage at all, baker. The text says discord broke out between the herdsmen of Abram and the herdsmen of Lot (Genesis 13:7). Lot is the one traveling with Abram. Laban is a different name from a different story, so keep him in your back pocket for later.

Kinsmen! Abram says it plainly: "After all, we are kinsmen." (Genesis 13:8) They're family, and he doesn't want a fight over where the cows graze. I think that's wise. Some arguments cost way more than they're worth.
Strangers would be a different story, friend. Abram says, "After all, we are kinsmen." (Genesis 13:8) That means relatives, so it's family business. The reason to keep the peace is the family tie.
No enemies here, baker. Abram tells Lot, "After all, we are kinsmen." (Genesis 13:8) He's talking to family, not a rival. The text shows Abram trying to protect that tie.

To the right! Abram says, "If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left." (Genesis 13:9) He lets Lot choose first and then goes the other way. Clean split, no fighting over the map.

If they both went left, they'd be stuck in the same crowd again, wouldn't they? Abram says, "If you go to the left, I will go to the right…" (Genesis 13:9) The whole point is to separate. Opposite directions, friend.

Abram doesn't say straight ahead. His words are, "If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left." (Genesis 13:9) Left and right are the only two choices on the table. He's making it simple on purpose, I think.

Well watered is exactly it. Genesis 13:10 says Lot saw that the whole plain of the Jordan, all the way to Zoar, was well watered. For people with huge herds, that's a big deal. Water is how you keep a lot of animals going.
Dry and rocky is the opposite of what he sees, baker. The text says the whole plain of the Jordan was well watered (Genesis 13:10). No dust-bowl here. That's what makes it look so good to Lot.
The text doesn't say anything about forest, friend. What Lot sees is that the plain of the Jordan was well watered (Genesis 13:10). Water is the detail that stands out. Trees aren't mentioned.

Egypt it is! Genesis 13:10 says the plain was well watered like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt. Abram and Lot had just come from there, so they knew it. That's a pretty big compliment for a stretch of land.

Moab is a nearby land, but the writer doesn't pick it. He says the plain was like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt (Genesis 13:10). Abram and Lot had just left Egypt, so that comparison would land. Keep your eye on that one.

Edom's a good guess for a place on the map, baker, but it's not in this verse. Genesis 13:10 says the plain was well watered like the garden of the LORD, like the land of Egypt. Egypt is the one the writer names. I'd bet Abram and Lot remembered it well.

Careful, friend, that one's backwards. The writer's note says, "This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah." (Genesis 13:10) So when Lot looks out, the cities are still standing. The destruction comes later.

False is right. The writer adds, "This was before the LORD destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah." (Genesis 13:10) So the destruction hasn't happened yet when Lot looks out. It's a little heads-up from the writer, and I'll leave it right there.
East! Genesis 13:11 says Lot chose the whole plain of the Jordan for himself and set out toward the east. He picks and he goes. Then the two of them part company.
West is a good guess, but the text says Lot set out toward the east (Genesis 13:11). He chose the whole plain of the Jordan and headed that way. Check your compass, baker.

North isn't it, friend. Genesis 13:11 says Lot chose the whole plain of the Jordan and set out toward the east. North and south come up later, when the LORD tells Abram to look around (Genesis 13:14). Lot's headed east.

True, and it's a serious line. Genesis 13:13 says the men of Sodom were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD. Lot pitched his tent toward that city (Genesis 13:12). The writer just says it plainly and moves on.

The text says the opposite, baker. Genesis 13:13 says the men of Sodom were wicked, sinning greatly against the LORD. That comes right after we hear Lot pitched his tent toward Sodom (Genesis 13:12). It's a heavy line, and the writer doesn't soften it.

Offspring, yes! The LORD says, "for all the land that you see, I will give to you and your offspring forever." (Genesis 13:15) It's a promise for Abram and for those who come after him. That's a long gift.
Servants isn't the word, friend. The LORD says, "I will give to you and your offspring forever." (Genesis 13:15) Offspring means his descendants. It's a promise that reaches way down the line.

The herdsmen are the ones who were arguing earlier (Genesis 13:7), but they're not in this promise. The LORD says, "I will give to you and your offspring forever." (Genesis 13:15) Offspring means Abram's descendants. Same land, bigger promise.

An altar to the LORD, yes! Genesis 13:18 says that's what Abram built at Hebron, near the Oaks of Mamre. He worshiped at the first altar and he builds another one at the new spot. Wherever he lands, that's where he turns to the LORD.

A well would be handy with all those animals, baker, but that's not what the text says. Abram built an altar to the LORD (Genesis 13:18). It's the same thing he did back at Bethel (Genesis 13:4). Worship first.

A watchtower sounds like a smart idea, but it's not here, friend. Genesis 13:18 says Abram built an altar to the LORD. That's the one building the text mentions at Hebron. He's got his tent up, and now he's got his altar.
